analysis.one_liner: Protects people who travel to other states for legal abortion and reproductive care from interference.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from June 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, several states enacted laws restricting abortion. This bill would make it unlawful for any person or government to punish, restrict, or discriminate against someone who travels to another state for reproductive health care that is legal there, or who helps someone make that trip. It would also protect out-of-state providers, let the Justice Department and private individuals sue to enforce the protections, and override conflicting state laws.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in states that restrict abortion and need to travel to obtain legal reproductive care, along with the clinics, doctors, and helpers who assist them. The bill's protections against lawsuits, prosecution, and retaliation would shield patients, providers, and aid organizations from state enforcement actions.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to restrict, sanction, or discriminate against anyone who travels to another state for reproductive health care legal in that state, or who assists with such travel.
Lets the Justice Department sue states or officials who enforce interfering laws, and gives patients, helpers, and providers their own right to sue, with damages and attorney's fees available.
Overrides state laws that conflict with its protections, waives state sovereign immunity, and lets defendants move interfering state-court cases to federal court.

analysis.who_pays: States that restrict abortion would lose their ability to enforce those restrictions against out-of-state travel, providers, and helpers. Anti-abortion legal organizations and state officials pursuing such enforcement would face lawsuits and liability.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on Congress's constitutional power to protect the right to travel and regulate interstate commerce; state officials and opponents argued federal preemption of state abortion enforcement exceeds those powers, and courts could have narrowed or struck provisions.

Its protections cover only reproductive care legal in the state where it is provided, so the bill would not restore abortion access in states that ban it; patients would still need to travel, a cost barrier that falls hardest on low-income people.

The private right of action with fee-shifting against states could generate extensive litigation against state governments and officials, a burden supporters of state restrictions viewed as improper federal overreach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for people in abortion-restricting states: legal protection for travel and for the helpers and clinics who make that travel possible. The bill does not create abortion access where it is banned, so its help depends on being able to travel, which costs money and time. The main trade-off is constitutional and federalist: it would strike down state laws in this area and open states to suits, which opponents consider an overreach. The cost is real but confined to states' ability to enforce restrictions against out-of-state care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 20, 2023 by Sen. Cortez Masto with 36 original cosigners and read twice before referral to the Judiciary Committee.
The bill's only action after introduction was its committee referral; no markup, vote, or floor consideration followed.
It accumulated 40 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, and never advanced in a chamber where Republicans held 49 of 101 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States with abortion restrictions and the officials and organizations enforcing them are better off because the bill never advanced; their laws remain in force. People who must travel for care remain without federal statutory protection, though courts have separately provided some protection.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 36 original cosigners.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup or vote from June 2023 through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored; the bill did not advance in the 118th Congress, in which Republicans held 49 seats and could sustain opposition.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would shield clinics, doctors, and aid groups from state penalties and lawsuits for serving out-of-state patients or funding travel.
They would lose the ability to enforce their restrictions against out-of-state travel, providers, and helpers, and would face suits and fee awards for violating the federal rule.

industries.industry: Crisis pregnancy centers and anti-abortion legal groups
industries.note: Their enforcement and litigation efforts against out-of-state abortion care would become unlawful and actionable.
